variants.title: Publish an object safely
variants.context: Publish an object through a commit protocol: authorize the intended key, upload parts, complete and verify, publish the version ID into authoritative application state, then clean provisional state.
variants.prompt: A 5 GB video is uploaded. Put the commit protocol in order.

items.text: Authorize the intended key with size, content type, checksum algorithm, and retention.
Upload parts under one upload ID with per-part checksums and bounded retries.
Complete the multipart upload and verify final size and checksum.
Commit the returned version ID into authoritative application state.
Abort abandoned uploads and reconcile ambiguous commits.

variants.hint: Parts are provisional until completion and application publication both succeed.
variants.explanation: Authorize → upload → complete and verify → publish the version → reconcile. Readers must never race an ambiguous “latest” object.

variants.title: Publish an object safely
variants.context: Publish an object through a commit protocol: authorize the intended key, upload parts, complete and verify, publish the version ID into authoritative application state, then clean provisional state.
variants.prompt: A completion call times out. Put the protocol in order, ending with how the timeout is handled.

items.text: Bind the key, limits, and checksum algorithm before accepting bytes.
Transfer parts with stable part numbers and receipts.
Issue the completion request and treat its timeout as ambiguous.
Query the object version and checksum, then commit the verified version to application state.
Abort or clean provisional parts that never completed.

variants.hint: An ambiguous completion is resolved by querying, not by guessing.
variants.explanation: Treat a timeout during completion as unknown until the object version is queried and reconciled with application metadata.

variants.title: Publish an object safely
variants.context: Publish an object through a commit protocol: authorize the intended key, upload parts, complete and verify, publish the version ID into authoritative application state, then clean provisional state.
variants.prompt: Two writers could target the same key. Put the safe protocol in order.

items.text: Authorize an immutable, generated key for this upload.
Complete with a conditional request and capture the entity tag.
Publish the exact version ID in application metadata.
Reconcile any record whose object commit is unknown.

variants.hint: Generated immutable keys and conditional writes prevent lost updates.
variants.explanation: Conditional writes and immutable keys stop two writers from silently overwriting each other. The application defines version selection.

variants.title: Drop the filesystem assumption
variants.context: Object APIs replace or create whole values. Rename may be copy plus delete, prefixes are not directories, and locks, directory transactions, and filesystem permissions do not appear automatically.
variants.prompt: A job renames a million objects into a new prefix and takes hours. Why?
options: Rename is typically copy plus delete per object, not one atomic namespace operation.
The bucket is throttled by name length.
Prefixes must be created first.
optionFeedback: Object stores do not move bytes with a directory rename.
Name length is not the cost driver here.
Prefixes are part of keys, not directories to create.
variants.hint: Is there a directory to rename?
variants.explanation: Plan key layouts up front. Moving objects means copying bytes and deleting the originals.

variants.title: Drop the filesystem assumption
variants.context: Object APIs replace or create whole values. Rename may be copy plus delete, prefixes are not directories, and locks, directory transactions, and filesystem permissions do not appear automatically.
variants.prompt: A service appends log lines to an object every second. What should it expect?
options: In-place append semantics differ by service; many replace the whole value.
Appends are always atomic and cheap.
The object grows like a local file.
optionFeedback: Verify append, overwrite, and conditional behavior for the chosen implementation.
No universal append guarantee exists across object stores.
Object APIs usually create or replace whole values.
variants.hint: What do object APIs usually operate on?
variants.explanation: Object storage works on whole objects. Batch log lines into appropriately sized objects instead of appending.

variants.title: Drop the filesystem assumption
variants.context: Object APIs replace or create whole values. Rename may be copy plus delete, prefixes are not directories, and locks, directory transactions, and filesystem permissions do not appear automatically.
variants.prompt: Two processes rely on a directory lock to coordinate writes to a bucket. What is missing?
options: Locks and directory transactions do not exist automatically; use conditional writes or an external coordinator.
Nothing; buckets support POSIX locks.
A longer timeout.
optionFeedback: Coordination needs conditional requests or a service that provides locking.
Filesystem locking semantics do not apply.
Timeouts do not create mutual exclusion.
variants.explanation: Coordinate through conditional writes, immutable keys, or an explicit coordination service.

variants.title: Recover the right version
variants.context: Replication and backup solve different problems: a valid delete or corrupt overwrite replicates normally. Versioning preserves history; immutable retention blocks selected mutations for a declared period.
variants.prompt: A script deletes a production prefix, and the deletion replicates to the second region. Why did replication not protect the data?
options: Replication copies valid operations, including deletes; it is not a backup.
Replication was misconfigured.
The second region was offline.
optionFeedback: A valid delete or corrupt overwrite replicates normally.
Replication did exactly what it does.
Being online is why it replicated.
variants.hint: What does a replica do with a valid delete?
variants.explanation: Replication provides another serving location. Versioning, independent backups, and retention provide recovery.

variants.title: Recover the right version
variants.context: Replication and backup solve different problems: a valid delete or corrupt overwrite replicates normally. Versioning preserves history; immutable retention blocks selected mutations for a declared period.
variants.prompt: Compliance requires that audit logs cannot be altered for seven years. Which control?
options: Immutable retention for the declared period.
Cross-region replication.
A lifecycle rule to a cheaper tier.
optionFeedback: Retention blocks selected mutations, including deletes, during the period.
Replication copies mutations; it does not block them.
Tiering changes cost, not mutability.
variants.hint: Which control prevents a mutation rather than copying it?
variants.explanation: Immutable retention prevents deletion or overwrite during the declared window; versioning alone keeps history but not a guarantee.

variants.title: Recover the right version
variants.context: Replication and backup solve different problems: a valid delete or corrupt overwrite replicates normally. Versioning preserves history; immutable retention blocks selected mutations for a declared period.
variants.prompt: After a malicious overwrite, the team restores files directly over production keys. What did they skip?
options: Restoring into a controlled namespace, validating the application, then cutting over explicitly.
Nothing; overwriting is fastest.
Enabling versioning first.
optionFeedback: Validate the pre-incident version before publishing it through a cutover.
Restoring over live keys can overwrite evidence and race with automation.
Versioning helps selection, but the restore procedure is what was skipped.
variants.hint: What should happen between selecting a version and serving it?
variants.explanation: Stop writers, select an authoritative version from time and integrity evidence, restore into a controlled namespace, validate, then cut over.

variants.title: Bound the access
variants.context: Use short-lived workload identities scoped to exact operations and prefixes. Pre-signed URLs delegate one method on one key for a short time. Keep the origin private behind a CDN or controlled gateway.
variants.prompt: A mobile client must upload one file to one key within ten minutes. Which mechanism?
options: A pre-signed URL for that method and key with a short expiry.
Embedding a long-lived bucket credential in the app.
Making the bucket public-write.
optionFeedback: A signed URL delegates one operation on one key for a bounded time.
Broad credentials in a client leak.
Public write invites abuse and cost.
variants.hint: What is the smallest capability that gets the job done?
variants.explanation: Pre-signed URLs delegate exactly one method on one key briefly; bind content limits where supported.

variants.title: Bound the access
variants.context: Use short-lived workload identities scoped to exact operations and prefixes. Pre-signed URLs delegate one method on one key for a short time. Keep the origin private behind a CDN or controlled gateway.
variants.prompt: Public images are served straight from a public bucket. What is the safer layout?
options: A private origin behind a CDN with origin access control.
A public bucket with logging.
Signed URLs for every image.
optionFeedback: Keep the origin private and let the CDN fetch with a controlled identity.
Logging observes exposure; it does not prevent it.
Signing every public image adds cost without a privacy need.
variants.hint: Who should be allowed to read the origin directly?
variants.explanation: Keep the origin private behind a CDN or controlled gateway, and validate cache keys so private content is never shared.

variants.title: Bound the access
variants.context: Use short-lived workload identities scoped to exact operations and prefixes. Pre-signed URLs delegate one method on one key for a short time. Keep the origin private behind a CDN or controlled gateway.
variants.prompt: A batch job needs to read one dataset prefix nightly. Which identity?
options: A short-lived role scoped to read on that prefix.
A permanent admin key.
The developer’s personal credentials.
optionFeedback: Scope to exact operations, buckets, and prefixes with conditions.
Admin keys are broad and long-lived.
Personal credentials tie production to a person.
variants.hint: Scope by operation, bucket, and prefix.
variants.explanation: Workload identity should be short-lived and narrow; log denials and policy changes.

variants.title: Estimate the physical footprint
variants.context: Versioning, replicas, incomplete multipart uploads, and small-object overhead multiply the physical footprint beyond the logical data. Physical bytes = logical bytes × versions retained × replicas, plus provisional parts.
variants.prompt: Logical data is 10 TB. Versioning retains three versions per object on average, and the bucket replicates to one other region. What is the physical footprint?
variants.hint: Multiply logical bytes by versions retained, then by copies.
variants.explanation: 10 × 3 versions × 2 regions = 60 TB of physical storage.

mistakes.feedback: That counts versions but forgets the replicated copy.
That counts the replica but forgets the retained versions.
Versions and replicas multiply the logical size.

variants.title: Estimate the physical footprint
variants.context: Versioning, replicas, incomplete multipart uploads, and small-object overhead multiply the physical footprint beyond the logical data. Physical bytes = logical bytes × versions retained × replicas, plus provisional parts.
variants.prompt: Logical data is 4 TB with two retained versions per object and no replication. Abandoned multipart parts add another 0.5 TB. What is the physical footprint?
variants.explanation: 4 × 2 = 8 TB, plus 0.5 TB of incomplete uploads = 8.5 TB. Abort stale uploads to reclaim that half terabyte.

mistakes.feedback: Incomplete multipart parts occupy space until aborted.
Two retained versions double the logical bytes.

variants.title: Estimate the physical footprint
variants.context: Versioning, replicas, incomplete multipart uploads, and small-object overhead multiply the physical footprint beyond the logical data. Physical bytes = logical bytes × versions retained × replicas, plus provisional parts.
variants.prompt: A lifecycle policy moves 70% of a 20 TB dataset to a cheaper tier. How many TB remain in the immediate tier?
variants.explanation: 20 × 0.3 = 6 TB stay in the immediate tier. Model retrieval delay and request charges for the 14 TB that moved.

mistakes.feedback: That is the amount moved; the question asks what remains.
The policy moved most of the data.
